messages:
rachel: FYI ran into a subtle flow when combining Retrofit suspend calls, OkHttp retries, and coroutine cancellation on Android. End result: what looked like duplicated POSTs in server logs.
glen: interesting. do you have a repro?
rachel: yes. App does a suspend call to upload metadata + kick off server-side processing. User navigates away -> coroutine cancelled -> we call cancel on the Retrofit call. Meanwhile the transport saw a transient ECONNRESET and OkHttp retried under the hood and the server accepted two requests (same payload). The coroutine cancellation didn't prevent the earlier retry flow that was already in-flight.
pete: oh that fits with OkHttp semantics. cancelling the call after the socket write started can leave the server with partial state, and an automatic retry can replay if the body is repeatable. Did you use idempotency keys?
rachel: we didn't. Our endpoint isn't strictly idempotent (creates a job). Server accepted two jobs, which caused duplicate work. Repro steps: 1) start upload via Retrofit suspend adapter; 2) simulate connection reset; 3) coroutine scope cancelled (user navigates away); 4) OkHttp does internal retry or authenticates and resends; server receives two full POSTs.
glen: two-pronged mitigation: client-side and server-side. Client: make requests idempotent (Idempotency-Key header) or disable retryOnConnectionFailure for non-idempotent endpoints. Server: dedupe by idempotency key or detect duplicate payloads.
rachel: For Android SDK samples I added: - a helper to attach a generated idempotency key per logical operation and show server sample that ignores duplicate idempotency keys - recommended OkHttp config snippet - a note about coroutine cancellation ordering. Code snippets: 
```kotlin
// generate idempotency key per user action
val idempotencyKey = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
val call = api.createJob(body).withHeader("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey) // pseudo
// OkHttp config suggestion for non-idempotent endpoints
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
  .retryOnConnectionFailure(false) // avoid hidden replays for non-repeatable bodies
  .connectTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
  .writeTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
  .build()
```

pete: good. Also call out dispatcher and maxRequests — if a canceled coroutine doesn't close the socket quickly, a queued retry might run later. For uploads you might want a dedicated Dispatcher with maxRequests=2 to avoid bursts.
glen: another nuance: Retrofit suspend adapter will map cancellation to call.cancel(), but if cancellation happens after the body has been written and connection closed, the retry path may still trigger. We should add an explicit check in our wrapper: when coroutine is cancelled, set a flag to prevent automatic retry or close the request body early. Hard to do generically though.
rachel: For the SDK docs I wrote a short section "Handling cancellations + retries on mobile": - Prefer idempotency keys for job-creating endpoints. - If using streaming bodies, either make them file-backed or mark endpoint non-retriable and set retryOnConnectionFailure=false. - Add a runtime warning when a suspend call is cancelled but the OkHttp client has retryOnConnectionFailure=true and the request body isn't repeatable.
pete: Nice. Could also include a quick server snippet showing idempotency handling: store key -> return 409 or stored response if repeated.
sdk-bot: Created issue #4333: "android-sdk: add idempotency-key examples and cancellation+retry docs for Retrofit coroutines" https://github.com/redwood-inference/android-samples/issues/4333 :robot_face:
rachel: I'll open a PR with sample toggles: useIdempotencyKey=true, retryOnConnectionFailure=false for non-idempotent flows, and an instrumented test that cancels the coroutine mid-upload and asserts only one job is created on fake server. Tagging @glen @pete for review. Thanks :thumbsup:
